title: My day
verifiedBy: LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Russian has ONE present tense where English has two. Ya rabótayu covers both "I work" (every day) and "I am working" (right now), and there is no second shape to reach for. Everything on this rung is a habit, and the same forms would do for what is happening this minute.

Verbs come in two ending patterns and the pattern is a property of the verb, learned with it — there is no way to tell from the meaning. Pattern I: rabótayu · rabótayete · rabótayet, chitáyu · chitáyete · chitáyet. Pattern II: govoryú · govoríte · govorít. The difference shows in the you-form and the he/she-form: -ete for one pattern, -ite for the other.

Some verbs write yó in their endings — p'yu · p'yóte, vstayú · vstayóte — and the acute on it is spelling rather than a stress decision: the Russian letter behind yó (ё) is by definition the stressed vowel of its word, so it can never be anything else. Write yó, never a plain yo and never e. The quiet Russian line keeps the two dots that most Russian printing drops and expects you to supply — and the acute in the romanization is telling you the very thing those missing dots would have told you.

The times of day are single words: útrom (in the morning), dnyóm (in the afternoon), vécherom (in the evening), nóch'yu (at night). They are frozen shapes of útro, den', vécher and noch' — the leftovers of a case this level does not teach — so learn them as they are and do not try to build them. They usually open the sentence.

Clock time is v plus the hour, and the word for "hour" changes with the number in front of it: odín chas, dva chasá, sem' chasóv. That is your first sight of a rule M8 will spell out — after 1 the noun is in its plain shape, after 2–4 it takes one ending, after 5 and up another. Here, just learn chasóv with the bigger numbers.

This level always writes the subject pronoun. Russian can drop ya, because the ending already names the person, and in speech it often does — but the drop is a stylistic judgement rather than a rule, and M5's past tense will not name the person at all. Keep the pronoun until you can hear when to lose it.

words.note: "I get up", from vstavát' — one Russian word for English's two, no separate "up". The you- and he/she-forms write yó: vstayóte, vstayót — and yó is always the stressed vowel.
Early. It describes the verb rather than a noun, so it never changes shape — a whole class of Russian words that ask nothing of you.

sentences.trap: English "get up" is a verb plus a little word, and hunting for the Russian "up" is wasted effort. vstayú is the whole thing.
sentences.sound: ya fsta-YOO RA-na. The v at the start is said as an f, because the s after it is voiceless — Russian consonants take their colour from their neighbours.

variations.changed: swap the time word — the verb does not move
vstayú → vstayóte for the polite you, and the yó appears in the ending
the he/she ending — vstayót, with the same yó

mistake.why: vverkh is a real word for "upwards", and it has no business here. vstayú already means "get up".

sentences.usage: Describing your routine — the first line of any "my day" conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: One Russian word swallows the English verb and its little word whole.

sentences.cue: I get up at seven o'clock

words.note: One preposition, two jobs here. Now it points at a clock time — v sem' chasóv, "at seven". In M7 it points at a place — v magazíne — and bends the word after it, as iz does.
Seven. The ' on the end is not a sound of its own — it softens the m. Numbers from five upward all end this way.
"Hour", and the number in front decides its shape: odín chas, dva chasá, sem' chasóv. English leaves "o'clock" untouched; Russian makes the noun answer to the number (M8).

sentences.trap: The noun changes because of the number, which English never does. "Seven o'clock" and "one o'clock" use the same word; sem' chasóv and odín chas do not.
sentences.sound: ya fsta-YOO f syem chee-SOF. The v is said as an f here too, and the final v of chasóv is an f as well — Russian ends words voiceless.

variations.cue: I get up at six o'clock
variations.changed: swap the number — chasóv stays, because six is also above four

variations.cue: I get up at two o'clock
variations.changed: dva takes the other ending: chasá, not chasóv

variations.cue: Do you get up at seven?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, asked rather than told

mistake.why: chas is the shape that goes after odín. After sem' it is chasóv.

sentences.usage: Any time of day — the frame every appointment and every routine runs on.
sentences.mnemonic: The number is in charge. The noun does what it is told.

sentences.cue: In the morning I drink tea

words.note: "In the morning", one word: no preposition, no article. A frozen shape of útro from a case this course does not teach — learn it whole. It normally opens the sentence.
"I drink", from pit'. The ' in p'yu and p'yóte is a separator keeping p and the vowel apart — "pyoo", not "pu". The you- and he/she-forms carry yó, the stressed syllable.

sentences.trap: "In the morning" is three English words and one Russian one, with nothing standing in for "in" or "the". Building it out of v plus útro is the English reflex and it is wrong.
sentences.sound: OO-tram ya pyoo chai. The unstressed o of útrom flattens to "a", and p'yu is one syllable, not two.

variations.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
variations.changed: swap the drink — neither word around it moves

variations.cue: In the evening I drink tea
variations.changed: swap the time of day — the frame is the same for all four

variations.cue: Do you drink tea in the morning?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, and the time word moved to the end — both orders are ordinary

mistake.why: There is no preposition in this phrase. "In the morning" is útrom, one word, and building it out of v plus útro is the English habit.

sentences.usage: Anything you do at a particular time of day — the spine of a routine.
sentences.mnemonic: Four times of day, four single words, no prepositions anywhere.

sentences.cue: In the evening I read a book

words.note: "In the evening", one word, the same frozen shape as útrom. Russian's evening runs from about five until properly dark; nóch'yu takes over after that.

sentences.trap: knígu still carries M3's object ending. A time word at the front changes nothing about what happens at the back of the sentence.
sentences.sound: VYE-che-ram ya chee-TA-yoo KNEE-goo. Three of the four vowels in vécherom are unstressed and flatten right down; only the first is fully said.

variations.cue: In the evening I read a newspaper
variations.changed: swap the thing read — and it bends the same way, being feminine too

variations.cue: In the evening I don't read
variations.changed: ne in front of the verb, and the object dropped altogether

variations.cue: Do you read in the evening?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, with the time word at the end

mistake.why: kníga is the subject shape. As the thing being read it is knígu — M3's ending, still doing its job.

sentences.usage: Evening routines — and the frame takes any of M3's verbs.
sentences.mnemonic: The front of the sentence and the back of it mind their own business.

words.note: "Every day", learned as one phrase. kázhdyy is "every" and den' is "day" — masculine, which is why kázhdyy ends the way it does. The phrase normally sits at the end of the sentence.

sentences.trap: Russian's one present tense is doing double duty here. Ya rabótayu kázhdyy den' is a habit, and Ya rabótayu on its own could be either "I work" or "I am working right now" — the time word is what settles it.
sentences.sound: ya ra-BO-ta-yoo KAZH-dy dyen'. The zh of kázhdyy is the s in English "measure"; the ' at the end of den' softens the n without adding a sound.

variations.changed: swap the verb — the phrase hangs off any of them
ne in front of the verb, and the phrase does not move
the polite you-form — pattern I, so the ending is -ete

mistake.why: The phrase is fixed and singular: kázhdyy den', one day at a time, however many of them there are.

sentences.usage: Routines, jobs, habits — and the single most useful time phrase on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: Every day, one day: Russian counts them one at a time.

words.note: Often. Words like this go in front of the verb in Russian, where English usually puts them after it or at the end. Never changes shape.

sentences.trap: The word order is the delta: Russian says "I often read" and English says "I read often". Both orders exist in English; only one is ordinary in Russian.
sentences.sound: ya CHA-sta chee-TA-yoo. The t of chásto is barely said between the s and the o — a cluster Russian smooths over.

variations.changed: swap the verb — chásto keeps its place in front of it
ne in front of chásto, because it is chásto that is being denied
the polite you-form, as a question

mistake.why: Understandable, and it puts the emphasis on "often" rather than saying it plainly. The neutral order is Ya chásto chitáyu.

sentences.usage: Saying how much you do something — chásto, vsegdá and inogdá all sit in the same slot.
sentences.mnemonic: How often comes before what you do.

words.note: Always, and it takes the same slot as chásto, in front of the verb. Note the spelling: it is written vsegdá and said "fsyeg-DA" — the v is an f here, as it is in vstayú.

sentences.trap: It looks like it should start with a v sound and it does not. Russian's v takes the voicing of whatever follows, and s is voiceless.
sentences.sound: ya fsyeg-DA pyoo KO-fye. The stress lands right at the end of vsegdá, which is unusual enough to be worth remembering.

variations.changed: swap the verb — vsegdá keeps its place in front of it

variations.cue: In the morning I always drink coffee
variations.changed: a time word in front, and vsegdá still hugs the verb
the polite you-form, with the yó in the ending

mistake.why: That order puts a strange emphasis on "always" and sounds foreign. It belongs in front of the verb: Ya vsegdá p'yu kófe.

sentences.usage: Habits you never break — and the ordinary way to answer "do you always …?".
sentences.mnemonic: vsegdá, chásto, inogdá: all three live in the same seat, in front of the verb.

words.note: "You speak", from govorít' — the other ending pattern: -ite for you and -it for he or she, where rabótat' took -ete and -et. Which pattern a verb takes has to be learned with it.
"In Russian", said of how you speak — a different word from M1's rússkiy yazýk, the language as a thing. After govorít' always this shape: govoríte po-rússki.

sentences.trap: M1's rússkiy yazýk cannot be used here. Vy govoríte rússkiy yazýk is the word-for-word English and it is wrong: speaking a language takes the po-rússki shape.
sentences.sound: vy ga-va-REE-tye pa-ROO-skee. Two unstressed o letters in govoríte, both flattened to "a", and the pitch rises on po-rússki.

variations.changed: govoríte → govoryú: the answer, in the I-form of pattern II
ne in front of the verb — the most useful sentence a beginner owns
the he/she ending of pattern II — govorít, not govorét

mistake.why: That is the English sentence with Russian words in it. Speaking a language takes po-rússki: Vy govoríte po-rússki?

sentences.usage: The most useful question a beginner can ask, and the most useful answer they can give.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not speak a language in Russian — you speak Russian-ly.

words.cue: in the afternoon · during the day
words.note: The frozen shape of den', roughly noon to early evening — not English "afternoon". Written with yó always, and the acute rides with the letter: dnyóm carries one where chas does not.

sentences.trap: It does not mean "in the day" as opposed to "in the night". dnyóm is the middle stretch of the day, sitting between útrom and vécherom — four parts, not two.
sentences.sound: dnyom ya ra-BO-ta-yoo. One syllable, and it opens with a d and an n together — a cluster English never starts a word with.

variations.changed: swap the verb — the time word keeps its place at the front

variations.cue: In the afternoon I don't work
variations.changed: ne in front of the verb; the time word is untouched

variations.cue: Do you work in the afternoon?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, with the time word moved to the end

mistake.why: The same English habit as V útro: there is no preposition in these phrases. It is dnyóm, one word.

sentences.usage: The middle of the day — the piece of a routine English speakers most often get wrong.
sentences.mnemonic: Four words for four parts of the day, and none of them needs a preposition.

words.note: The last of the four, frozen from noch'. Russian's night starts late — around midnight in ordinary use — so somebody arriving at ten in the evening arrives vécherom, not nóch'yu.

sentences.trap: splyu is M3's spat' with its everyday ending, and it grows an l the way lyublyú does. The dictionary shape gave no warning of it.
sentences.sound: NO-chyu ya splyoo. Both words end in a soft sound — the yu does the softening in each — and neither is more than one syllable of real weight.

variations.changed: ne in front of the verb, and the time word does not move
the polite you-form of pattern II — spíte, with the time word at the end
the he/she ending — spit, another pattern II verb

mistake.why: spat' is the dictionary shape and only goes after another verb (Ya khochú spat'). Standing on its own it needs an ending: Nóch'yu ya splyu.

sentences.usage: Closing a description of your day — and the last of the four time words.
sentences.mnemonic: The dictionary shape waits behind another verb; on its own, the verb has to say who.

comprehensionPool.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
In the afternoon I read a book
Do you drink coffee in the morning?

comprehensionPool.display: Ya vsegdá vstayú v sem' chasóv.
comprehensionPool.script: Я всегда встаю в семь часов.
comprehensionPool.cue: I always get up at seven o'clock
